ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two spheres with radii $36$ and one sphere with radius $13$ are each externally tangent to the other two spheres and to two different planes $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$. The intersection of planes $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ is the line $\ell$. The distance from line $\ell$ to the point where the sphere with radius $13$ is tangent to plane $\mathcal{P}$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows two planes P and Q meeting along a line ell, forming a dihedral wedge. Three spheres lie in this wedge, with two larger spheres and one smaller sphere; they are arranged so that each sphere is tangent to both planes and externally tangent to the other spheres. Reasoning: Take a coordinate cross-section perpendicular to ell. In that cross-section, the two planes become two rays forming an angle, and let θ be the half-angle of the wedge. A sphere of radius r tangent to both planes has its center on the angle bisector. Its center is distance r csc(θ) from ell, and its tangency point on plane P is distance r cot(θ) from ell. The two radius-36 spheres have the same cross-sectional center position, so their tangency to each other must occur by separation along ell; since their radii sum to 72, their centers are 72 apart along ell. Put them symmetrically at ell-coordinates +36 and -36. The radius-13 sphere is tangent to both large spheres, so by symmetry its ell-coordinate is midway, namely 0. For the distance between a radius-36 center and the radius-13 center, the total center distance is 36 + 13 = 49. The along-ell component is 36. The cross-sectional component is the difference of their angle-bisector distances: 36 csc(θ) - 13 csc(θ) = 23 csc(θ). Therefore 49^2 = 36^2 + (23 csc(θ))^2. Thus (23 csc(θ))^2 = 2401 - 1296 = 1105, so csc^2(θ) = 1105/529. Then cot^2(θ) = csc^2(θ) - 1 = 1105/529 - 529/529 = 576/529, so cot(θ) = 24/23. The desired distance from ell to the tangency point of the radius-13 sphere on plane P is 13 cot(θ) = 13 · 24/23 = 312/23. Hence m = 312 and n = 23, so m + n = 335.

Let the half-angle between the two planes in this cross-section be theta. A sphere of radius r tangent to both planes has its center on the angle bisector at distance r csc(theta) from ell, and its point of tangency with plane P is at distance r cot(theta) from ell. The two radius-36 sphere centers have the same cross-sectional position, so because they are externally tangent their separation along ell is 72. Place them symmetrically, so the radius-13 center is midway along ell. For a radius-36 sphere and the radius-13 sphere, the center distance is 49, with along-ell component 36 and cross-sectional component (36-13)csc(theta)=23 csc(theta). Thus 49^2=36^2+(23 csc(theta))^2. Solve to get cot(theta)=24/23. Therefore the desired distance from ell to the radius-13 sphere's tangency point on P is 13 cot(theta)=312/23, so m+n=335.

method.method_draft: Work directly in plane P using the tangency points of the spheres with P. Orthogonally project each sphere center to P; the projected points are exactly the P-tangency points. For two externally tangent spheres of radii a and b both tangent to P, the distance between their tangency points in P is sqrt((a+b)^2-(a-b)^2)=2 sqrt(ab), because their centers differ normally to P by |a-b| and are separated by a+b. Thus the two radius-36 tangency points are 72 apart, while the radius-13 tangency point is 12 sqrt(13) from each large tangency point. These three points form an isosceles triangle in P with base 72 and equal sides 12 sqrt(13), so the altitude from the small point to the base is sqrt((12 sqrt(13))^2-36^2)=24. Now use the fact that tangency to Q forces the distance from ell to a radius-r tangency point on P to be r times the same constant t=cot(theta). Hence the two large tangency points are at distance 36t from ell and the small one at distance 13t; their perpendicular separation in P is 23t. So 23t=24, and the desired distance is 13t=312/23, giving m+n=335.

raw_record.original_question: Two spheres with radii 36 and one sphere with radius 13 are each externally tangent to the other two spheres and to two different planes, \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\). The intersection of planes \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\) is the line \(\ell\). The distance from line \(\ell\) to the point where the sphere with radius 13 is tangent to plane \(\mathcal{P}\) is \(\frac{m}{n}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. Find \(m+n\).
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows two planes P and Q meeting along a line ell, forming a dihedral wedge. Three spheres lie in this wedge, with two larger spheres and one smaller sphere; they are arranged so that each sphere is tangent to both planes and externally tangent to the other spheres. Reasoning: Take a coordinate cross-section perpendicular to ell. In that cross-section, the two planes become two rays forming an angle, and let θ be the half-angle of the wedge. A sphere of radius r tangent to both planes has its center on the angle bisector. Its center is distance r csc(θ) from ell, and its tangency point on plane P is distance r cot(θ) from ell. The two radius-36 spheres have the same cross-sectional center position, so their tangency to each other must occur by separation along ell; since their radii sum to 72, their centers are 72 apart along ell. Put them symmetrically at ell-coordinates +36 and -36. The radius-13 sphere is tangent to both large spheres, so by symmetry its ell-coordinate is midway, namely 0. For the distance between a radius-36 center and the radius-13 center, the total center distance is 36 + 13 = 49. The along-ell component is 36. The cross-sectional component is the difference of their angle-bisector distances: 36 csc(θ) - 13 csc(θ) = 23 csc(θ). Therefore 49^2 = 36^2 + (23 csc(θ))^2. Thus (23 csc(θ))^2 = 2401 - 1296 = 1105, so csc^2(θ) = 1105/529. Then cot^2(θ) = csc^2(θ) - 1 = 1105/529 - 529/529 = 576/529, so cot(θ) = 24/23. The desired distance from ell to the tangency point of the radius-13 sphere on plane P is 13 cot(θ) = 13 · 24/23 = 312/23. Hence m = 312 and n = 23, so m + n = 335.

The geometric claims about centers lying on the angle bisector, equal-radius centers sharing the same cross-sectional position, symmetry along ell, and the distance calculation are all valid under the diagram's same-wedge interpretation. No revision is needed.
推理整体正确，结论与标准答案一致，并且基本严格遵循指定方法。可小幅加强的一点是：在使用“两个大球切点连线平行于 \(\ell\)”时，最好明确说明两个半径为 36 的球在平面 \(\mathcal P\) 上的切点位于 \(\ell\) 同侧且到 \(\ell\) 距离相同，因此它们落在同一条与 \(\ell\) 平行的直线上；这样可避免该桥接步骤显得略跳跃。
